FINAL NATURAL-LANGUAGE HYPOTHESIS (one paragraph; descriptive of this sample only):

"Restricting to the 7,099 white respondents in this NLSY-79-based sample (3,469 males, 3,630 females) and measuring wealth with the supplied composite wealth variables, within-sex wealth inequality — the headline dimension — rose substantially between 1990 and 1996 for both white males and white females: the P90/P50 ratio more than doubled for males (13.8 → 37.5) and roughly tripled for females (12.1 → 37.6), the P95/P50 ratio rose from about 22 to 62 for males and 18 to 60 for females, the share of respondents holding zero wealth roughly doubled (males 25.7% → 43.3%, females 20.3% → 42.6%), and the bottom-coded-at-zero Gini increased modestly for both sexes (males 0.780 → 0.793; females 0.761 → 0.777), while the top-decile wealth share stayed essentially flat (≈0.62 males, ≈0.59 females). This widening dispersion was driven by a collapsing lower middle — medians fell about 43% for males (15,601 → 8,900) and 56% for females (20,100 → 8,825) as zero-wealth respondents surged past two in five — alongside fast-growing upper-tail wealth (means rose to about 132k for males and 129k for females). In contrast, the secondary male–female wealth-gap dimension narrowed dramatically over the same window: the female-favorable 1990 median gap of about $4,500 (female median 20,100 vs male 15,601) closed to near parity by 1996 (8,900 vs 8,825), and the mean gap flipped from female-favorable (−11,442) to slightly male-favorable (+2,956), a swing driven by both sexes' middles collapsing rather than by any male gain in relative position. All of these statements are descriptive of this sample; the data support no causal claims."

(Direction-of-change statements and the full per-metric table are in the evidence and artifacts below.)

payload.hypothesis: Restricting to the 7,099 white respondents in this NLSY-79-based sample (3,469 males, 3,630 females) and measuring wealth with the supplied composite wealth variables, within-sex wealth inequality rose substantially between 1990 and 1996 for both white males and white females: P90/P50 more than doubled for males (13.8 to 37.5) and roughly tripled for females (12.1 to 37.6), P95/P50 rose from ~22 to ~62 (males) and ~18 to ~60 (females), the zero-wealth share roughly doubled (males 25.7% to 43.3%; females 20.3% to 42.6%), and bottom-coded-at-zero Gini increased modestly for both sexes (males 0.780 to 0.793; females 0.761 to 0.777) while the top-decile share stayed flat (~0.62 males, ~0.59 females); this widening was driven by a collapsing lower middle (medians fell ~43% for males and ~56% for females as zero-wealth respondents exceeded two in five) alongside fast-growing upper-tail wealth. In contrast, the male-female wealth gap narrowed dramatically: the female-favorable 1990 median gap of ~$4,500 closed to near parity by 1996 (8,900 vs 8,825) and the mean gap flipped from female-favorable (-11,442) to slightly male-favorable (+2,956). These statements are descriptive of this sample only and support no causal claims.
payload.workflow: Loaded data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv (12,013 rows, 0 missing values); restricted to race=='white' (n=7,099: male 3,469 / female 3,630). For each sex-year computed mean, median, P90/P50, P75/P50, P95/P50, bottom-coded-at-0 Gini, positive-only Gini, top-5%/top-10% wealth shares, and % zero/negative/non-positive; percentile ratios restricted to positive denominators (P10=P25=0 everywhere made P90/P10 and P75/P25 undefined). Bootstrap 95% CIs (2,000 reps) for bottom-coded Gini. ever_jailed=0 rerun as sensitivity (dropping 69 jailed whites; no material change). composite_wealth_1985 used only as a one-line background note. All statistics descriptive and unweighted.
